name: Carlos Garcia

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time, Carlos. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government, and we're not selling anything. Everything you tell me stays confidential, so feel free to tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run an extrusion line at a plastic pipe plant on the edge of town, past the church of Saint Anne. Plastic pellets go into a heated barrel, get pushed out through a die as a long pipe, cooled in a water bath and cut to length. I watch the temperatures, check the wall thickness with a gauge and change dies when we switch sizes. My dad worked at that plant for thirty-one years, and some of the men still call me 'young Garcia'. I like it, it's honest work, but the smell of hot plastic stays in your clothes.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What's life like outside the plant?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm engaged to Lucia, we're getting married in the spring at Saint Anne's, where my parents married. She works at her family's bakery. I've got about eight months saved, and my grandfather left me a piece of land outside town with some old olive trees, which I go and look after on Saturdays. Sunday is church and lunch with the family, always.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, it's all talk from people who sell computers. I'd say it at work and at Sunday lunch. I don't really go online, apart from the football results.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd be very happy. I've never touched any of these AI things and I don't want to. My dad did thirty-one years on that line with a pencil and a gauge, and I'd like to do the same.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing different. Get married in the spring, keep saving, keep working. Maybe start building a small house on my grandfather's land in a few years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm and content. It's how things should be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Has anyone at the plant tried to bring in new technology?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They put in a new screen on line three that's meant to adjust the temperatures itself. It keeps getting it wrong in winter, and old Benito has to override it. So no, I'm not impressed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would building on the land mean to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Everything. A house where my kids can grow up near the olive trees, close to my parents and Lucia's. That's what I work for.

S0.say: I'd say I told you so, it was all talk from people selling computers. I'd say it at work and at Sunday lunch rather than online.
S0.think: Honestly, I'd be very happy, because I've never touched AI and I don't want to. I'd like to work that line for decades, the way my dad did.
S0.do: Carries on as normal: marries in the spring, keeps saving and keeps working. Plans to build a small house on his grandfather's land in a few years.
S0.feel: Calm and content, as things should be.
S0.quote: My dad did thirty-one years on that line with a pencil and a gauge, and I'd like to do the same.
S0.fieldNote: Carlos's identity is tied to family, faith and following his father into the plant. He's suspicious of new tech, backed up by a self-adjusting screen that doesn't work. The land his grandfather left him is central to his future.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say companies have the right to run their business how they want, that's the free market. But I'd also say a good company looks after its people, like this plant did for my dad. I'd say it to the managers if I had the chance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be uneasy. Extrusion lines are already half automatic, and if they add robots for the cutting and the packing, they'll need fewer of us. I'd hope my years there count for something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing my job well and keep my head down. I'd save a bit more, maybe cut back on the wedding a little. I'm not going to go learning computers, but if the company wanted to train me on the new line, I'd do it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Like a cloud over the wedding.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you turn to if your job changed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Family first. My uncle runs a small building firm, and my dad knows everyone at the plant. In my family, if one of us is in trouble, the others turn up with a van and a cooked meal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd cut back on the wedding. What goes first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The second band Lucia's mother wanted. One is plenty. The church and the meal stay, those aren't negotiable.

S1.say: I'd say companies have the right to run their business as they want, but a good company looks after its people, as this plant did for my dad.
S1.think: I'd be uneasy, because extrusion is already half automatic and robots for cutting and packing would mean fewer of us. I'd hope my years there count for something.
S1.do: Keeps working hard, saves a bit more and trims the wedding budget, dropping a second band. Would accept company training on a new line but won't seek out tech skills himself.
S1.feel: Uneasy, like a cloud over the wedding.
S1.quote: In my family, if one of us is in trouble, the others turn up with a van and a cooked meal.
S1.fieldNote: Carlos balances free-market views with a belief that good companies owe loyalty. His safety net is family rather than the state. He's willing to train if asked, but only if asked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's wrong, and the people building these things have no idea what work means to a man or a family. I'd say we don't want handouts, we want work. I'd say that at church, at work, to anyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd be frightened. The plant would go robotic fast, and every other plant nearby too. I'd have savings and the land, but I'd be a married man with no trade that anyone wants.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut back hard, save everything, and talk to Lucia about whether we still marry in the spring or wait. I'd lean on my family, my uncle's building firm, my dad, the parish. I wouldn't take any government money unless there was no other choice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd be praying a lot, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you wouldn't take government money. What if your savings ran out?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd take it, but I'd be ashamed. My grandfather would turn in his grave if he saw me queueing for a cheque because a machine took my job. I'd try everything else first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two years isn't long. Would you try to learn anything new?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I wouldn't know what. If the robots can do anything, then they can build houses too, so my uncle's firm won't last either. I'd hold on to what I have and trust in God and my family.

S2.say: I'd say it's wrong and the people building this don't understand what work means to a family. We don't want handouts, we want work.
S2.think: I'd be frightened, because my plant and every other plant nearby would go robotic fast. Even with savings and the land, I'd be a married man with no trade anyone wants.
S2.do: Cuts back hard, saves everything and discusses delaying the wedding with Lucia. Leans on his family, his uncle's building firm and the parish, and avoids government money unless there's no choice.
S2.quote: My grandfather would turn in his grave if he saw me queueing for a cheque because a machine took my job.
S2.fieldNote: Carlos's sharpest fear is losing his role as a provider, which matters more to him than the money. He would accept state help only as a last resort and with shame. Faith and family are his main support.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need to keep jobs for people, and companies should take apprentices, not just buy robots. I'd say the government should support families, not just give out money. I'd say it to the priest and anyone who'd listen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, five years feels hardly any better. Lucia and I want children soon, and I'd be thirty-two with maybe a baby. I can't see how I'd learn a whole new trade in that time with a family to feed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working and save hard, put off building on the land. I'd lean on family and the parish for help with anything we needed. And I'd wait to see what happens, because I don't know what else I could train for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Still alarmed. It's the same fear, just slower.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would five years change your plans for children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It might. I'd want children, God willing, but I'd want to know I could feed them first. Lucia and I would talk about waiting a couple of years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you need to see to change your mind about learning something new?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Someone showing me a trade the robots won't touch, and a real apprenticeship, with a master and a wage. Not a computer course. If that existed, I'd do it.

S3.say: I'd say we need to keep jobs for people, and companies should take apprentices instead of just buying robots. The government should support families, not just give out money.
S3.think: Five years feels hardly any better, because Lucia and I want children soon. I can't see how I'd learn a whole new trade while starting a family.
S3.do: Keeps working, saves hard and postpones building on the land. Leans on family and the parish and waits to see what happens, though he'd take a real apprenticeship if one existed.
S3.feel: Still alarmed, the same fear only slower.
S3.quote: I'd want children, God willing, but I'd want to know I could feed them first.
S3.fieldNote: The extra three years barely help Carlos because they overlap with his plans for marriage and children. He'd only consider a traditional apprenticeship with a master and a wage. His resistance comes from caution more than stubbornness.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is time to build things properly, with families and churches and local businesses, not just governments. I'd say young people should learn real trades. And I'd say the companies owe something back to the towns that made them rich.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, ten years feels better. I'd be thirty-seven. I could work at the plant for a few more years, save hard, and build on my grandfather's land.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working and saving for the first few years. I'd invest in the land, plant more olive trees, maybe a vegetable plot, so at least we'd have food and a bit to sell. And I'd keep close to the family and the parish.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but less. Like I'd have time to put my house in order, literally.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why the land, in a world where robots can farm too?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because land is land. Robots can pick olives, maybe, but they can't make that land mine any more than it already is. Whatever happens with jobs, a family with land and food is not helpless.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still avoid AI tools, even with ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably, yes. I know that might be foolish. But I'd rather be good with olive trees than with computers.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is time to build properly with families, churches and local businesses, not just government. Young people should learn real trades, and companies owe something back to their towns.
S4.think: Ten years feels better. I could work at the plant a few more years, save hard and build on my grandfather's land by the time I'm thirty-seven.
S4.do: Keeps working and saving for the first few years, then invests in the land with more olive trees and a vegetable plot. Stays close to family and parish and still avoids AI tools.
S4.feel: Anxious, but less so, with time to put his house in order.
S4.quote: Robots can pick olives, maybe, but they can't make that land mine any more than it already is.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years, Carlos's plan centres on his grandfather's land and self-reliance. He admits his avoidance of AI might be foolish but sticks with it. The land offers him a sense of dignity as well as security.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because it comes right as I'm getting married and starting a family. I'm not afraid of hard work, I'm afraid of having no work to be good at. What would help is real apprenticeships with a wage, and help for families, not just a cheque in the post.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about faith. For me, that's a big part of how I'd get through it. Whatever happens with jobs, I'd still have God, my family and my land.

headlineQuote: I'm not afraid of hard work, I'm afraid of having no work to be good at.
portrait: Carlos is a 27-year-old extrusion line operator at the plastic pipe plant where his father worked for thirty-one years. He's engaged, goes to church every Sunday, has about eight months saved and owns his grandfather's land with old olive trees. He has never used AI and doesn't want to, leaning on family and parish rather than the state. Calm in the plateau, he becomes alarmed in both faster AGI pictures because they collide with his wedding and plans for children. With ten years his answer is to invest in the land and build a self-reliant family life.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most because it would arrive just as he marries and starts a family, leaving no work to be good at.
whatWouldHelp: Real apprenticeships with a wage, and support for families rather than just a cheque in the post.
